opus-5.5.text:
For me, a moonshot is legitimate when three things are true. Failure is a real possibility, but even the failure teaches the world something.

First, the goal has to be clearly defined, even if it's very hard. "Build AGI" is too vague to falsify. "Build an AI system that can produce verified, novel mathematics" is ambitious, and you know whether you've done it or not. In math you have something rare: a ground truth. A proof checks or it doesn't. That makes the moonshot honest, because you can't hide behind demos or vibes.

Second, there has to be a credible reason why now. Many moonshots fail because they're too early. The technology underneath isn't ready, so you're pushing a boulder uphill. When I look at AI for math, several curves are crossing at once. Language models have gotten good at reasoning. Formal languages like Lean have matured, and there's a growing library of formalized mathematics. And reinforcement learning works much better when you have a perfect verifier. Any one of those alone isn't enough. Together they make something possible that wasn't five years ago.

Third, and maybe most important, the intermediate artifacts have to be valuable. If you aim for the moon and land on a mountaintop, is the mountaintop worth something? For us, even if we never get to a fully autonomous mathematician, the steps along the way matter. Better autoformalization, better verified code generation, tools that help human mathematicians check their work: those have real value. Formal verification connects to chip design, to software security, to anywhere correctness really matters. So the downside isn't zero.

On the financial risk, I think investors in this space understand the bargain. You're buying a probability distribution, not a guaranteed outcome. What you owe them is to be rigorous about the distribution. Don't pretend the risk isn't there. Show the milestones, be honest when something isn't working, and build a team that could pivot the technology if the biggest version doesn't pan out.

And frankly, someone has to try. If every capable team only works on things that are 90% likely to succeed, we never get the big jumps. I'd rather spend my twenties on something that, if it works, changes how humanity does science, than on something safe that wouldn't matter much either way.

r001.rationale: The response never discusses whether success changes how an ambitious venture is labeled as a moonshot or a bubble.

r002.rationale: It says failure is possible, can teach the world, and that someone should try, but does not advocate an environment that tolerates failure.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention pension savers or the possibility that layered investment ultimately makes them fund researchers’ curiosity.

r004.rationale: It describes the mission’s potential to change science, but does not identify commitment to the mission rather than personal ego as a basis for legitimacy.

r005.rationale: It mentions building a team that could pivot, but not researchers joining forces instead of making fragmented attempts at the same problem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "legitimate" is doing a lot of work in that question, so let me take it apart a bit.

A moonshot is legitimate to me when it's aimed at a problem that actually matters if you succeed, and when there's a real reason the moment is now rather than five years ago or five years from now. For us at Axiom, that problem is mathematical reasoning. Math is the one domain where you can verify truth completely, with a proof checker like Lean, and that changes the economics of training. You don't need a human in the loop to tell you whether the model got it right. So you get this closed loop where the model proposes, the verifier checks, and the signal is clean. That's a technical argument for why now, and if someone can't give you that kind of argument, I'd be skeptical.

The second thing is that the failure mode has to be informative. If we spend years and hundreds of millions of dollars and it doesn't work, we should still have learned something the field didn't know. A moonshot that fails silently, where nobody can say what was wrong, is closer to gambling. A moonshot that fails and tells you "this bottleneck is real, here's where it broke" is research, just done at a scale that only a company can fund.

The financial risk is real and I don't want to minimize it. But I'd push back on the framing a little. The expected value calculation for something like automated mathematics is strange because the upside isn't incremental. If you get a system that can genuinely do new math, that compounds into physics, into engineering, into verification of software and hardware. So the right question isn't "what's the probability of failure" in isolation, it's whether the probability times the magnitude justifies the attempt. For a small number of problems, I think it clearly does.

And honestly, the last piece is the people. A legitimate moonshot is one where the people working on it would be doing something adjacent anyway, in academia or at a lab, and the company is just the vehicle that lets them do it faster and with more compute. If the team is there because it's the current hot narrative, that's a tell. If they were obsessed with the problem before anyone would fund it, that's the one I'd bet on.

astra-6.text:
I think the financial risk alone doesn’t tell you whether a moonshot is worth attempting. The questions are: if it works, does it create something genuinely valuable? And is there a credible reason to believe this team can make progress toward it?

You don’t need certainty—that would defeat the point of a moonshot—but you do need a technical thesis, a way to test it, and the willingness to change your mind when the evidence goes against you. Ambition shouldn’t exempt you from accountability.

And the people funding it should understand the risk they’re taking. A company can fail financially and still have been a serious, legitimate attempt. What matters is whether it was honest about the uncertainty and disciplined about trying to resolve it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the probability of failure from the quality of the attempt. A company can be very likely to fail and still be worth building if the problem matters, there’s a credible technical approach, and the team can explain what evidence would change its mind.

For me, the key question is: what would have to be true for this to work, and how are you testing that? There should be concrete milestones that reduce uncertainty, even if the ultimate ambition is enormous. And you have to be honest with the people taking the risk—employees and investors—about what’s demonstrated and what’s still a hypothesis.

A moonshot is legitimate when the ambition comes with that discipline. The possibility of a huge outcome isn’t, by itself, a justification for spending money.
